description: Red Canary highlights that despite falling payment rates, ransomware operators continue to drive payout demands higher year over year — sustaining the criminal economy through volume and exfiltration-only extortion.
quote: "Ransomware continues to surge year-over-year, and payout demands are only getting higher."

title: Exfiltration-only extortion groups
description: Threat groups abandoning encryption entirely in favor of pure data-theft extortion. These groups rely on living-off-the-land techniques to steal data and threaten public disclosure, reducing operational complexity.

title: Key CVEs exploited by ransomware actors
description: Red Canary tracked three high-impact CVEs leveraged by ransomware affiliates in 2025: a SonicWall VPN flaw exploited by Akira nearly a year after patches were available, and two Veeam vulnerabilities used for initial access and privilege escalation.

title: macOS stealer families ranked
description: Relative prevalence of macOS stealer families in 2025. Atomic Stealer led throughout the year, followed by Odyssey (rebranded from Poseidon). MacSync and Phexia emerged late in 2025, with DigitStealer as the least-distributed newcomer.

title: macOS attack surface expanding
description: As enterprise Mac fleets grow, attackers have followed — porting paste-and-run tradecraft from PowerShell to shell scripts and AppleScript. Red Canary urges tailored macOS detection strategies.
quote: "As more employees switch to Macs, the macOS-specific attack surface for your organization expands, requiring a new tailored approach to defense."

title: Primary identity attack vectors
description: Red Canary identifies six dominant identity attack categories observed in 2025. Infostealers and credential exposure feed downstream brute-force and consent-phishing campaigns, while MFA bypass tactics including AitM kits and MFA fatigue are growing fastest.

title: Adversaries automating with AI
description: Red Canary observed adversaries integrating AI services, command-line tools, and MCP servers into their tradecraft to automate reconnaissance, credential theft, and data exfiltration — accelerating the operational tempo of intrusions.
quote: "Adversaries are leveraging AI services, command-lines tools and MCP servers to automate reconnaissance, credential theft, and data exfiltration."

title: Notable vulnerable software in 2025
description: Software ecosystems Red Canary specifically tracked during 2025 due to exploited vulnerabilities: SAP NetWeaver, Microsoft Windows Server Update Services (WSUS), and SharePoint. All three saw active exploitation by financially motivated and state-aligned actors.

title: Customers in detection telemetry
description: Red Canary's 2026 Threat Detection Report synthesizes detections across more than 1,000 customer environments spanning endpoints, networks, cloud infrastructure, identities, and SaaS applications.

title: Paste-and-run dominates delivery
description: ClickFix and FakeCAPTCHA paste-and-run techniques became the dominant initial-access vector for stealers in 2025, pairing with loaders such as HijackLoader, MintsLoader, and CypherIT to deliver LummaC2 and Rhadamanthys.
quote: "Paste and run techniques (ClickFix/FakeCAPTCHA) were the dominant distribution vector for stealers in 2025."

title: Identity vs endpoint detection share
description: Identity-based detections (53%) overtook endpoint detections (estimated 47%) in 2025 for the first time in Red Canary's history, signaling a structural shift in where defenders must focus their resources.

title: Charcoal Stork malvertising cluster
description: Charcoal Stork emerged as a prevalent malvertising threat, delivering payloads more serious than typical adware. Red Canary linked it to related malware ChromeLoader and SmashJacker, which together formed an interconnected malvertising ecosystem.

title: RMM tools as ultimate payload
description: Red Canary observed remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools — including NetSupport Manager (rank #4) — increasingly delivered as the final payload of phishing and web-based campaigns rather than as auxiliary tooling.
quote: "In 2025, Red Canary observed RMM tools as the ultimate payload in an increasing number of campaigns, including web-based phishing."

title: 35.5% of 2024 breaches originated from third parties
description: SecurityScorecard's STRIKE team analyzed 1,000 data breaches and found that at least 35.5% (355 cases) involved a third-party nexus in 2024, up 6.5 percentage points from 29% in 2023. The figure is likely conservative since many third-party origins go unreported.

title: Third-party breach share rose 6.5 points YoY
description: The share of all breaches involving a third-party nexus climbed from 29% in 2023 to 35.5% in 2024, reflecting attackers' shift from direct intrusions toward exploiting vendor, supplier and software-provider relationships.

title: Fourth-party breaches reached 4.5% of all incidents
description: Of 1,000 breaches analyzed, 45 cascaded into a fourth party — accounting for 4.5% of all breaches and 12.7% of third-party breaches. A single compromise increasingly triggers widespread disruption across multiple organizations.

title: Third-party breach rate by industry
description: Retail & Hospitality (52.4%) is the only industry where a majority of breaches involve third parties. Tech/Telecom (47.3%), Energy & Critical Infrastructure (46.7%) and Travel/Logistics (45.3%) all exceed the 35.5% global average, while Education sits at 11%.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Third-Party Breaches by Industry

title: 52.4% of Retail & Hospitality breaches come via third parties
description: Retail, Hospitality, and Consumer Goods is the only industry where third-party compromises form the majority of breaches (52.4%). It moves from fifth in overall breach volume (10.3%) to second in third-party breach share (15.2%), driven heavily by payment-card ecosystems and e-commerce vendor dependencies.

title: 46.7% of Energy & Critical Infrastructure breaches are third-party
description: Energy, Utilities, and Critical Infrastructure represents only 3% of all breaches but 46.7% of its breaches (14 of 30) flow through third parties — mirroring SecurityScorecard's prior U.S. energy supply chain analysis where 45% of breaches had third-party connections.

title: Healthcare leads breach volume but below-average third-party rate
description: Healthcare, Pharmaceuticals, and Biotechnology accounts for 24.2% of all breaches (242 incidents) and 22% of third-party breaches (78 incidents) — the highest raw counts in both metrics. Yet just 32.2% of its breaches are third-party, below the 35.5% global average, because attackers find direct routes into healthcare more viable.

title: Third-party breach rate by region
description: Northeast Asia is the only region where more than half of all breaches (54.3%) involve third parties. Oceania (43.2%) and Europe (38.8%) also exceed the global average (35.5%), while North America — despite holding 59% of all breach volume — sits below at 31.9%.

title: North America: 59% of breach volume, 31.9% third-party rate
description: North America dominates total breach volume at 59% of all breaches and 53% of third-party incidents (188 cases), yet its third-party rate (31.9%) falls below the 35.5% global average — largely because U.S. healthcare disclosure laws inflate direct-attack counts.

title: Country third-party breach rates: affluent nations on top
description: Singapore (71.4%), the Netherlands (70.4%), Japan (60%) and Taiwan (57.1%) lead the world in third-party breach rate. The U.S. (30.9%) sits below the 35.5% global average. The Netherlands' rate was driven by a major breach at a customer-communications firm that cascaded through Dutch utilities and housing associations.

title: Singapore: 71.4% third-party breach rate — highest globally
description: Singapore posted the highest national third-party breach rate (71.4%) despite a small sample size, appearing alongside documented Chinese cyber operations targeting its overseas Chinese population and strategic position in regional economics and naval power projection.

title: Wealthier nations face higher third-party breach risk
description: SecurityScorecard finds a counterintuitive correlation: organizations in affluent economies invest more in security, so attackers shift to third-party vectors to circumvent stronger direct defenses. China, Brazil and Russia rank among the highest by overall breach share but disappear from the top third-party breach countries.
quote: "Affluent nations face disproportionately high third-party breach risks... attackers respond by seeking third-party vectors to circumvent stronger defenses."

title: Third-party breach enablers by category
description: Across 400 supply chain relationships involved in breaches, cross-industry software & IT leads at 37.5%, followed by industry-specific non-technical services (22%) and cross-industry non-technical services (13%). Technology overall enabled 46.75% — a notable drop from the ~75% reported in prior analyses, signalling diversification of attack surfaces.

title: Top 5 third-party breach vectors
description: File transfer software leads as the third-party breach vector at 14% of relationships, followed by cloud products & services (8.25%), foreign subsidiaries & acquisitions (7.75%), payment card data (7.25%) and pharmaceutical distribution/clinical trial support (7%).
pageOrSection: Products and Services at the Center of Supply Chain Risk

title: File transfer software share fell from 26% to 14% YoY
description: File transfer software remains the #1 third-party breach vector but its share of third-party relationships dropped from 26% in the prior year to 14% in 2024, even as C10p exploited Cleo zero-days at scale.

title: 63.5% of vulnerability-based breaches traced to two Cleo CVEs
description: C10p's exploitation of CVE-2024-50623 and CVE-2024-55956 in Cleo Harmony, VLTrader and Lexicom accounted for 54 of the 85 vulnerability-based third-party breaches (63.5%) in SecurityScorecard's dataset — a single campaign dominating the third-party vulnerability landscape.
comparison: Cleo campaign vs all vuln-based third-party breaches

title: Threat actor distribution: ransomware groups dominate
description: Across 315 attributable breaches, ransomware groups account for 64.8% of incidents, non-ransomware criminals and non-patriotic hacktivists 21.9%, and state-sponsored actors plus patriotic hacktivists 13.3%. Among third-party breaches specifically, the ransomware share climbs to 67.7%.

title: C10p drove 41.5% of attributable third-party breaches
description: C10p (Clop) ransomware was responsible for 41.5% of the 130 attributable third-party breaches in 2024, largely through file transfer software zero-days. The group also accounted for 17% of all attributable breaches — more than twice the next most active group.

title: Top third-party attack specialists
description: C10p ransomware leads at 41.5% of attributable third-party breaches, far ahead of miscellaneous ransomware groups (12.3%), Chinese state-sponsored actors (8.5%), miscellaneous criminals/hacktivists (7%) and UNC5537 (7% — the Snowflake campaign).

title: China is the most prolific state-sponsored third-party actor
description: Chinese state-sponsored groups drove 8.5% of attributable third-party breaches in 2024 — twice Russia's tally — with frequent supply chain targeting of Japan, Taiwan, the Philippines and Singapore. Chinese-attributed activity also exploited Ivanti Connect Secure VPN CVEs to breach MITRE and CISA.

title: 41.4% of ransomware/extortion attacks had a third-party nexus
description: Of 297 ransomware or extortion incidents in 2024, 123 (41.4%) had a third-party component — 5.9 points above the 35.5% baseline. Those 123 incidents represent 34.6% of all third-party breaches, confirming supply chain compromise is now a core ransomware strategy.

title: Foreign subsidiaries are 2x more likely than domestic to drive breaches
description: Subsidiaries and acquisitions account for 11.75% of third-party breach relationships globally. Foreign subsidiaries appear in 7.75% of breach relationships — nearly twice the domestic share (4%) — owing to language, time-zone, regulatory and integration gaps. In Japan, subsidiaries drive 33% of third-party breaches.

title: 27.5% of third-party breach relationships are Healthcare or Financial Services-specific
description: Industry-specific products and services in Healthcare (15.75%) and Financial Services (11.75%) together represent 27.5% of all third-party breach relationships — virtually unchanged from 28% the prior year, despite both industries running below-average third-party breach rates.
comparison: healthcare + finserv vectors vs all 400 relationships

title: Attackers are logging in through the back door
description: SecurityScorecard frames the 2024 third-party threat landscape as a strategic failure of perimeter-focused security — defenders look inward while adversaries scale through trusted vendor relationships.
quote: "More than 1 in 3 breaches (35.5%) now come through third parties — attackers aren't breaking in; they're logging in with your partners' credentials while you're busy patching your own systems."
pageOrSection: Don't let a third party reality check become checkmate

title: US share of ransomware attacks
description: The United States accounted for 41.42% of observed ransomware attacks in 2025, down from 53.30% in 2024. It remains the primary target country owing to its concentration of large organisations and stronger ransom payment capacity.

title: US share of Dark Web news
description: The United States dominated Dark Web news posts at 19.91% in 2025, a modest increase from 18.17% in 2024. The country's large digital footprint and high-value data assets keep it the most-mentioned target across underground markets.

title: Data and database threats dominate
description: Data and database related threats represented 64.06% of Dark Web activity, confirming that data theft is the primary driver of underground markets. Threat actors can easily prove legitimacy of stolen data through samples, making it the most monetisable asset class.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Threat Type

title: Selling posts dominate Dark Web news
description: Selling activity accounted for 59.32% of all Dark Web news posts in 2025, confirming that most underground activity is driven by direct monetisation goals. Sharing posts followed at 33.21%, often used by threat actors to build reputation.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Threat Categories

title: Public Administration most exposed industry
description: Posts mentioning Public Administration accounted for 12.85% of Dark Web news in 2025, the largest industry share. This is an upward trend from 11.17% in 2024, when the sector ranked third, reflecting sustained pressure on government institutions via data leaks.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Industry

title: Akira tops ransomware activity
description: Akira ransomware led 2025 activity with 8.35% of attacks, rising from outside the Top 3 in 2024 to the number one slot. Qilin and Cl0p followed closely, illustrating a fragmented but competitive ecosystem.

title: Stealer malware entry price
description: Information-stealer malware starts at just $15 on Dark Web markets, enabling mass adoption and large-scale credential theft. This subscription-based pricing also applies to bulk stealer logs, dramatically lowering the barrier to entry for cybercrime.

title: SMS spam services start at $0.05
description: SMS spam services are the cheapest offering observed on Dark Web markets, starting at just $0.05 per message. The ultra-low price point lowers the barrier for mass smishing campaigns and supports high-volume abuse.

title: Hacking has shifted from brilliance to opportunity
description: SOCRadar's analysts describe how today's cybercrime ecosystem rewards convenience over technical sophistication, with valid credentials traded openly on the Dark Web replacing complex exploit chains.
quote: "Over the years, hacking has transformed. It has shifted from being about technical brilliance and sophistication to something far simpler: leveraging opportunities. By purchasing valid credentials on the Dark Web, hackers bypass the need for complex exploits."

title: Ransomware market fragmentation
description: SOCRadar's analysts warn that the rise of Akira and a long tail of mid-tier groups have produced a fragmented ransomware ecosystem in which no single actor dominates, raising defender uncertainty.
quote: "Last year Akira Ransomware was not even in the Top 3 but in 2025 they took the first place. This fragmented threat landscape is increasing unpredictability and operational risk for defenders."

title: High-end zero-day average price
description: High-end zero-day exploits average $150,000 on Dark Web markets in 2025, down from $200,000 in 2024. Mid-tier zero-day prices have doubled to $20,000 while the low-end floor jumped from $100 to $1,000.

title: Oracle EBS zero-day sold for $70K
description: A threat actor offered a zero-day affecting Oracle E-Business Suite for sale on a Dark Web forum in June 2025 for $70,000. Months later, Cl0p ransomware launched a targeted campaign against Oracle EBS users, illustrating how traded zero-days move quickly into large-scale ransomware operations.

title: Dark Web threats by threat type
description: Data and database related threats dominate Dark Web activity at 64.06%, far ahead of access-related threats at 21.65%. Tools, services, website-related posts and vulnerability listings remain limited as those products are harder to produce.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Threat Type

title: Dark Web posts by activity category
description: Selling dominates Dark Web posts at 59.32% with sharing in second place at 33.21%, reflecting both monetisation goals and reputation-building. Hack announcements, partnership and buying posts remain marginal as future plans are rarely advertised on forums.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Threat Categories

title: Dark Web news by primary target country
description: The United States leads Dark Web news at 19.91%, followed by France, India and Indonesia at similar mid-single-digit levels. European countries including the UK, Spain and Germany maintain steady visibility, often linked to data leaks and fraud.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Primary Target Country

title: Dark Web threats by industry
description: Public Administration leads industry exposure at 12.85% of Dark Web posts in 2025, narrowly ahead of Information, Finance and Insurance which form a high-value cluster linked to data resale, fraud and extortion.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Dark Web Threats by Industry

title: Malicious software pricing range
description: Exploits command the highest prices on Dark Web markets at up to $5,000, while loaders and RATs cluster between $200 and $3,000. Stealers stand out with a $15 entry price thanks to subscription models, enabling mass adoption.

title: Zero-day pricing by tier, 2024 vs 2025
description: Low-end zero-day prices jumped from around $100 in 2024 to $1,000 in 2025, mid-tier doubled from $10K to $20K, while high-end zero-days fell from $200K to $150K. The shift reflects both improved exploit quality at the low end and increased availability at the high end.

title: DDoS and spam service pricing
description: DDoS attacks start at $20 and reach $600 while stressers stay slightly cheaper. Email services cost as little as $1 and SMS services start at $0.05, supporting high-volume low-skill abuse through subscription-based pricing.

title: Hacking services pricing
description: Antivirus disabling commands the highest price at $1,000 to $3,000, reflecting its value in bypassing defences. Droppers and malware encryption stay below $500, supporting repeated campaign use, with per-file dropper prices dropping even lower.

title: Phishing kits and templates pricing
description: Phishing panels and spoofers range from $50 to $500, accessible to low-skill actors. Scam pages show the widest range up to $2,000, reflecting customisation and brand-targeting demand for sophisticated cloned login pages.

title: Credit card pricing by region
description: US and UK credit cards command the highest prices on Dark Web markets at $5 to $50 due to acceptance rates and fraud success. European, Gulf and APAC cards cluster between $1 and $20, while African cards remain capped at $10 owing to limited fraud yield.

title: Online payment account pricing
description: Accounts on widely adopted services such as PayPal and Revolut average $100 thanks to high trust and merchant acceptance. Accounts on limited-adoption services like ZEN and P100 average $50 due to reduced fraud utility.

title: Personal data pricing
description: Core identity attributes such as mother's maiden name, driver's licence data and national ID numbers are priced between $5 and $10 because of their value for identity verification and account takeover. Contact-level data such as phone numbers and email addresses fetches just $1 to $5.

title: Money laundering service fees
description: Money laundering services on Dark Web markets are priced as a percentage of laundered funds. SOCRadar groups them into low-fee (2-5%), mid-range (5-10%) and high-fee (10-20%) categories reflecting complexity, operational risk and perceived reliability.

title: Social media account pricing
description: X (Twitter) accounts are the most expensive on Dark Web markets at $100 to $200 with verified accounts higher. LinkedIn accounts range from $10 to $100 for fraud and recruitment scams, while Facebook accounts hold steady at $50 to $75 and Amazon Business Prime accounts reach $100.

title: Stealer logs by target domain
description: Facebook and Google lead stealer log volumes by a wide margin, confirming their value across malicious operations. Gaming platforms like Roblox, Twitch and Epic Games drive high volume thanks to younger users with weaker credential hygiene, while PayPal stands out as a direct fraud enabler.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Stealer Logs by Domains

title: Stealer logs by country
description: India leads stealer-log volumes by a wide margin, reflecting large-scale malware spread and high credential reuse. Brazil and Indonesia follow, driven by consumer platforms and low endpoint protection, while the US ranks lower than expected likely due to faster detection and remediation.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Stealer Logs by Country

title: Ransomware attacks by affected country
description: The United States is the primary ransomware target at 41.42% of observed attacks in 2025, far ahead of any other country thanks to its concentration of large organisations and strong ransom payment capacity. Australia, Japan and the UK show moderate exposure tied to critical services and manufacturing.
pageOrSection: Distribution of Ransomware Attacks by Affected Country

title: Most active ransomware groups of 2025
description: Akira leads ransomware activity with 8.35% of attacks, followed closely by Qilin and Cl0p. The Top 10 actors together account for nearly half of ransomware incidents in 2025, signalling a fragmented but competitive ecosystem that complicates defender response.

title: New malicious OSS packages discovered in 2025
description: Sonatype identified more than 454,600 new malicious open source packages across npm, PyPI, Maven Central, NuGet, and Hugging Face throughout 2025. This represents a major escalation in industrialized supply chain attacks targeting developer ecosystems.

title: Cumulative known and blocked OSS malware
description: The total cumulative count of known and blocked malicious packages reached 1.233 million across npm, PyPI, Maven Central, NuGet, and Hugging Face by end of 2025. The figure reflects Sonatype's full historical detection corpus since 2019.

title: Open source malware YoY growth
description: Open source malware grew 75% year-over-year in 2025, as attackers industrialized campaigns and state-linked groups advanced from simple droppers and crypto miners to multi-stage payload chains.

title: Share of OSS malware hosted on npm
description: 99% of all open source malware identified in 2025 occurred on the npm ecosystem. JavaScript's enormous publishing volume, low barrier to entry, and tight integration with developer tooling make it the highest-velocity attack surface.

title: Trust at scale is the central engineering challenge
description: Sonatype frames the 2026 report's thesis: as software reuse accelerates and AI agents enter the dependency loop, the ability to verify components and remediate risks at planetary scale has overtaken raw productivity as the dominant concern.
quote: "Trust at scale is now the central engineering and business challenge of modern software."

title: OSS downloads across the four largest registries
description: Open source consumption hit 9.8 trillion downloads across Maven Central, PyPI, npm, and NuGet in 2025, a 67% increase year-over-year. The growth highlights the scale of dependency reuse driving both productivity and risk.

title: OSS download growth year-over-year
description: Aggregate downloads across Maven Central, PyPI, npm, and NuGet rose 67% year-over-year in 2025. The world did not just build more software but reused more of it, more often.

title: 2025 downloads by registry
description: npm dwarfs the other three registries in raw 2025 download volume, capturing roughly 81% of the aggregate. Maven Central and PyPI sit in a similar band, while NuGet trails the pack.

title: Year-over-year download growth by registry
description: npm led growth at 65.4% YoY, followed closely by PyPI at 50.6%. Maven Central and NuGet posted lower but still healthy double-digit growth, signalling continued mainstream adoption of Java and .NET dependencies.

title: Open source malware by threat category
description: Repository abuse and Potentially Unwanted Applications dominate the malicious package taxonomy in 2025, together accounting for over 83% of detected behaviours. Exfiltration, droppers, and backdoors form the next tier of high-impact tradecraft.

title: Lazarus Group malicious packages tracked
description: North Korea-linked Lazarus Group was attributed to 800+ malicious packages in 2025, with 97% concentrated on npm. The group advanced from droppers and crypto miners to five-stage payload chains targeting developers.

title: Lazarus Group package behaviour profile
description: Nearly every Lazarus package contained a dropper component, with secrets exfiltration appearing in roughly two-thirds and backdoor functionality in almost a third. The compositions are stacked, not exclusive — 77% of packages carried two or more threat types.

title: Packages compromised by Shai-Hulud worm
description: In September 2025 the first self-replicating npm malware, dubbed Shai-Hulud, compromised over 500 packages within days of release. The worm marked a tradecraft shift from single-package attacks toward autonomous propagation.

title: Malicious packages from IndonesianFoods campaign
description: The IndonesianFoods campaign generated 169,538 malicious packages, designed to self-replicate every seven seconds. It illustrates how modern OSS malware operates at machine speed against registries with weak abuse controls.

title: Open source CVEs lacking NVD CVSS scores
description: 65% of open source CVEs analysed in 2025 did not have an NVD-assigned CVSS score, leaving defenders without baseline severity context. When Sonatype scored those records, 46% rated as High or Critical.

title: Median NVD time-to-score open source CVEs
description: The NVD took a median of 41 days to score open source CVEs in 2025, with some taking up to a year. 47% of 2025 CVEs required more than 3 months to receive complete NVD records.

title: Vulnerability data quality issues
description: Comparing NVD records against Sonatype's enriched intelligence surfaced 167,286 false negatives — exploitable components that the public source failed to flag — alongside 20,362 false positives. The gap underscores the cost of relying solely on public CVE data.

title: Vulnerable Log4j downloads in 2025
description: Nearly 200 million vulnerable Log4j versions were downloaded in 2025, representing 13% of all Log4j downloads. Despite patches existing for years, organisations continue to pull known-bad versions into builds.

title: Vulnerable downloads that had fixes available
description: Approximately 95% of vulnerable component downloads in 2025 had a fixed version available upstream; only ~0.5% lacked any remediation path. The data reframes most software supply chain risk as an avoidable consumption problem.

title: GPT-5 dependency version hallucination rate
description: When operating without real-time intelligence, GPT-5 hallucinated 27.8% of component versions across 37,000 analysed upgrade recommendations — and in some cases suggested actual malicious packages. AI assistants are becoming a new vector for supply chain risk.

title: Maven Central traffic concentration by source
description: 108 billion of the 125 billion Maven Central requests in 2025 came from just the top three cloud service providers, versus 17 billion from all other users combined. The findings warn of fragile concentration in OSS distribution infrastructure.

title: EOL package versions with CVEs and no patch
description: Sonatype identified 81,000+ package versions that are both end-of-life and carry known CVEs, making them structurally unpatchable. Combined with 5–15% of enterprise dependencies being EOL, this represents a major hidden risk pool.

title: npm releases linked to CVSS 9.0+ vulnerabilities
description: 838,778 npm releases in 2025 were associated with vulnerabilities scored CVSS 9.0 or higher. The figure quantifies the critical-severity blast radius developers pull through their lockfiles.

title: OSS share of modern applications
description: Open source comprises 80–90% of the code in modern applications, making the dependency graph the dominant attack surface and the focal point of new regulatory regimes such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act.

title: Identity-related root causes drove 67% of incidents
description: Across 661 Sophos IR and MDR cases (Nov 2024 - Oct 2025), 67.32% of incidents were rooted in identity-related attacks - compromised credentials, brute force, phishing, auth-token theft or trusted-relationship abuse. Identity, not vulnerabilities, is the new front line.
comparison: vs vulnerability exploitation as historical leader

title: Median dwell time collapses to 3 days
description: Median attacker dwell time across all cases dropped to just 3 days, driven by both faster attackers and faster MDR detection. MDR cases sat at a 2-day median while IR cases ran 5 days, with non-ransomware IR cases the slowest at 6 days.

title: 88% of ransomware deployed during off-hours
description: Attackers deliberately time encryption events for nights, weekends and holidays when defender coverage is thinnest. 88.10% of ransomware payloads were deployed during non-business hours, with a slight bump on Thursday and Friday.

title: Attackers reach Active Directory in 3.4 hours
description: Median time from initial access to an attempt on Active Directory dropped to just 3.40 hours - a 70% acceleration over 2024. Once inside, adversaries beeline for the identity backbone faster than most SOCs can triage their first alert.

title: MFA missing or misconfigured in 59% of incidents
description: Nearly six in ten Sophos cases involved organizations where MFA was either disabled, never actually rolled out, or misconfigured in ways attackers could trivially bypass. The figure improved from 64% in 2024 but remains the largest single hygiene gap.

title: 51 distinct ransomware brands observed in one year
description: The ransomware ecosystem is fragmenting: Sophos counted 51 unique brands across cases, with 24 of them brand-new and 27 carried over from prior years. Only LockBit, Medusa, Phobos and BitLocker abuse have persisted continuously since 2020.

title: Akira accounted for 22% of ransomware incidents
description: Akira (Gold Sahara) dominated the 2025 ransomware landscape, present in 22.58% of incidents - more than double its nearest rival Qilin. The top five brands combined accounted for roughly half of all cases.

title: Half of stolen data leaked within 19.5 days
description: Of ransomware cases with confirmed exfiltration, 49.07% saw the stolen data publicly leaked within a median of 19.5 days. Confirmed exfiltration appeared in 49.77% of ransomware incidents, with another tranche unconfirmed but suspected.

title: Identity cannot be patched away
description: Sophos Field CISO John Shier on why identity, not vulnerability management, is now the defining battle of the incident-response landscape.
quote: "The dominance of identity-related root causes for successful initial access cannot be addressed by simple patch hygiene."

title: AI is not yet replacing attackers
description: Sophos found only one verified case of generative AI in attacker workflows during the reporting window. The lived reality contradicts forecasts of an imminent AI-driven attack revolution.
quote: "AI is adding scale and noise but not yet replacing attackers."

title: Root causes of incidents (2025)
description: Identity-rooted vectors - compromised credentials, brute force and phishing - together drove more than 60% of incidents. Vulnerability exploitation, long the headline cause, has been nearly matched by brute-force volume.

title: Median dwell time by case type
description: MDR cuts dwell time roughly in half versus IR engagements. Non-ransomware IR cases - typically stealthier intrusions like data theft or BEC - sit on the network longest.

title: Top industries hit (2025)
description: Manufacturing remains the dominant target, capturing roughly one in five Sophos cases. Financial services, construction, IT and healthcare round out the top five sectors.

title: Most active ransomware brands
description: Akira and Qilin pulled away from the pack in 2025, while SafePay, Inc and Play filled out the top five. Together the top five brands accounted for roughly half of all ransomware incidents Sophos investigated.

title: Most victims are small or mid-sized firms
description: 84% of Sophos cases involved organizations with fewer than 1,000 employees, and 56% had 250 or fewer. The ransomware economy is heavily weighted toward SMBs that lack 24/7 monitoring.

title: When attacks happen across the clock
description: Adversaries cluster work into late-night windows: 37.1% of all attacks land between 11pm and 3am, and the period from 6am to noon is the quietest. Defenders without 24/7 coverage are systematically blind during the busiest hours.

title: Impacket usage jumped 83% YoY
description: Impacket - the open-source Python toolkit for SMB and Kerberos abuse - now accounts for 36% of all attacker tooling observed by Sophos, an 83.08% surge over 2024. Python rides alongside as a required dependency.

title: One CVE drove 67% of exploit-based intrusions
description: CVE-2024-40766 in SonicWall SonicOS accounted for 67.31% of all confirmed CVE exploitations across Sophos cases - a stark reminder that a single unpatched edge appliance can dominate a year of incidents.

title: Median patch-to-exploit window: 322 days
description: Attackers exploited CVEs a median of 322 days after the patch was released - and 296.5 days after a public PoC. Defenders are losing patch races they have months to win.

title: Average time to exfiltration: ~79 hours
description: From first foothold to data leaving the network, Sophos saw a mean of 78.83 hours. Once exfiltration began, defenders typically detected it within 1.87 hours - but by then the data was already gone.

title: 40% of Windows Servers are end-of-life or close to it
description: 13% of Windows Server instances seen in Sophos cases were already end-of-life and 27% more were approaching EOL - a combined 40% of legacy identity infrastructure still anchoring production networks.

title: BEC cases up fourfold year over year
description: Business Email Compromise cases handled by Sophos quadrupled in 2025 as attackers leaned harder on session-token theft, MFA bypass and FlowerStorm-style phishing kits to ride identity into the inbox.

title: 661 cases across 70 countries and 34 industries
description: The 2026 Active Adversary Report draws on 661 IR and MDR engagements handled between Nov 2024 and Oct 2025, spanning 70 nations and 34 industry sectors - one of the broadest active-incident datasets in cybersecurity.

title: 79% of data exfiltration happens off-hours
description: 78.85% of confirmed data exfiltration events occurred outside of business hours, with a small bump on Wednesday and Thursday. Stealing data, like deploying ransomware, is overwhelmingly a night-shift activity.

title: Exploited vulnerabilities lead root causes
description: For the third year running, victims identified exploited vulnerabilities as the most common technical root cause of ransomware attacks. They were used to penetrate organizations in 32% of incidents in 2025.
pageOrSection: Why organizations fall victim to ransomware

title: Lack of expertise top operational gap
description: Lack of expertise — not having the skills or knowledge to detect and stop the attack in time — was the most common operational root cause cited by victims. It contributed to falling victim to ransomware in 40.2% of incidents.

title: Data encryption rate hits six-year low
description: Data encryption is at the lowest reported level in six years, with 50% of attacks now resulting in data encryption, down from 70% in 2024. This suggests organizations are increasingly capable of stopping attacks before the encrypted payload is deployed.

title: Data theft alongside encryption
description: 28% of organizations that had their data encrypted also experienced data exfiltration. Adversaries don't only encrypt data — they also steal it, with 14% of all ransomware victims reporting theft.

title: Vast majority recover encrypted data
description: 97% of organizations that had data encrypted were able to recover it. Just over half (54%) used backups while 49% paid the ransom to recover.

title: Ransom payment rate remains elevated
description: 49% of victims paid the ransom to get their data back. While this is a slight drop from last year's 56%, it remains the second highest ransom payment rate in six years.

title: Median ransom demand drops one-third
description: The median ransom demand fell 34% year-over-year, coming in at $1,324,439 in 2025 compared to $2 million in 2024. The drop was driven by a decrease in demands of $5M+, which fell from 30% to 24% of cases.

title: Median ransom payment cut in half
description: The median ransom payment fell 50% in the last year, down from $2 million in 2024 to $1 million in 2025. The primary driver is a reduction in payments of $5M or more, down from 31% in 2024 to 20% in 2025.

title: Victims paid 85% of initial demand on average
description: Among 826 organizations sharing both their initial demand and actual payment, victims paid on average 85% of the initial ransom demand. 53% paid less than the ask, 29% matched it, and 18% paid more.
pageOrSection: How actual payments stack up with the initial demand

title: Recovery cost falls 44% year-over-year
description: Excluding any ransom paid, the average cost to recover from a ransomware attack dropped 44% over the last year, coming in at $1.53 million, down from $2.73 million in 2024.

title: More than half recover within a week
description: Organizations are getting faster at recovering from ransomware attacks, with 53% fully recovered after a week — a significant jump from 35% in 2024. Almost all victims (97%) were fully recovered three months on from the attack.

title: Increased anxiety on cybersecurity teams
description: 41% of IT/cybersecurity teams say they have increased anxiety or stress about future attacks following a ransomware incident where data was encrypted. Every organization that had data encrypted reported direct repercussions for the team.

title: Encryption at lowest level in six years
description: Sophos researchers note a marked drop in attacks that resulted in data encryption, signaling improved defensive posture across surveyed organizations.
quote: "Data encryption is at the lowest level in six years, with 50% of attacks now resulting in data encryption, down from 70% in 2024."

title: Leadership replaced after attack
description: The human consequences of ransomware extend well beyond technical recovery — in a quarter of cases, IT/cybersecurity team leadership was replaced following the attack.
quote: "In one quarter of cases, the team's leadership was replaced as a consequence of the attack."

title: Technical root cause of attacks, 2023-2025
description: Exploited vulnerabilities lead as the top technical root cause for the third year running. Phishing rose sharply from 11% to 18%, while compromised credentials dropped from 29% to 23%.

title: Operational root causes of ransomware attacks
description: Victims typically face multiple operational challenges, citing 2.7 factors on average. Lack of expertise narrowly tops the list, followed by an unknown security gap and lack of people/capacity.

title: Data encryption outcome trend, 2020-2025
description: Tracks the share of ransomware attacks resulting in data encryption, stopped before encryption, and extortion-only (no encryption) over six years. Encryption rates dropped from 73% in 2020 to 50% in 2025, while extortion-only doubled to 6%.

title: Recovery via backups vs ransom payments, 2020-2025
description: Use of backups to restore encrypted data is at its lowest level in six years (54%), while the ransom payment rate of 49% remains the second highest in six years. The gap between the two recovery methods has narrowed considerably.

series.name: Paid ransom and got data back

title: Median ransom demand vs payment by company revenue
description: Ransom demands rise sharply with company revenue. The largest revenue organizations ($5B+) saw the greatest reduction, paying just 36% of the initial demand on average. Smaller revenue cohorts ($10-50M) paid 97% of the median demand.
comparison: demand vs payment by revenue band
pageOrSection: How actual payments stack up with the initial demand

title: Average ransomware recovery cost by company size
description: Recovery costs (excluding ransom paid) climb with organization size and plateau for companies between 1,001 and 5,000 employees. The smallest cohort (100-250) reports $638K while the largest cohort reports $1.83M.

title: Recovery time from ransomware attacks, 2022-2025
description: Organizations are recovering faster. The share of victims fully recovered within a day climbed from 8% in 2023 to 16% in 2025, while the within-a-week share jumped from 35% in 2024 to 53% in 2025.

title: Human consequences on IT/security teams
description: Every organization that had data encrypted reported direct repercussions for the IT/cybersecurity team. Top impacts include increased anxiety, pressure from senior leaders, and changes to team priorities or workload.

title: Total APT detections recorded
description: Trellix's Advanced Research Center logged 540,974 APT detections globally between April 1 and September 30, 2025. The figure underscores the scale of nation-state aligned activity tracked across the Trellix sensor network during the six-month window.

title: Unique APT campaigns tracked
description: Trellix identified 1,221 unique APT campaigns spanning the six-month observation period. The figure captures distinct clusters of activity rather than total detections, indicating the diversity of nation-state aligned operations.

title: Countries targeted by APT activity
description: APT campaigns observed by Trellix reached 121 countries across 14 sectors during April-September 2025. The geographic footprint reflects the global reach of state-aligned cyber operations.

title: Ransomware victim posts observed
description: Trellix counted 3,280 ransomware victim posts across leak sites between April and September 2025. The volume captures attacker-claimed victims and reflects extortion-focused activity.

title: Ransomware attacks up globally
description: Trellix noted ransomware attacks rose 41% globally in the August 2025 data point. The growth reflects continued aggression from affiliate networks despite the collapse of RansomHub earlier in the period.

title: Qilin's share of ransomware victim posts
description: Russian-speaking Qilin emerged as the dominant ransomware group with 441 victim posts, accounting for 13.45% of total ransomware activity. The rise followed the collapse of RansomHub in April 2025.

title: AI adoption inflection point
description: John Fokker, VP Threat Intelligence Strategy at Trellix, frames AI-enabled attack chaining as imminent. The quote anchors the report's central theme: automation and geopolitical malice converging.
quote: "As threat actors near the AI adoption inflection point, demonstrating more structured use of AI-powered attack methods, they'll be able to chain multiple AI-driven attacks with unprecedented fluidity."

title: Automation and geopolitical malice converge
description: Trellix's John Fokker captures the report's thesis: cybercriminal automation now operates alongside nation-state-aligned activity, requiring multi-layered detection across the kill chain.
quote: "We're seeing automation and geopolitical malice converge. Security teams should prioritize a defense-in-depth strategy, focusing on multiple detection opportunities."

title: Qilin ransomware target distribution
description: Qilin showed a clear preference for industrial organizations at 29.25% of their attacks, followed by consumer services and financials. The skew toward operational targets reflects extortion leverage from disruption risk.

title: Top-5 ransomware group concentration
description: The top 5 ransomware groups accounted for just 39.86% of attacks, indicating significant fragmentation across the affiliate ecosystem after the RansomHub collapse. Affiliates dispersed to Qilin, DragonForce, and emerging operators.

title: PowerShell-driven ransomware campaigns
description: PowerShell dominated ransomware tool-based activity, appearing in 719 campaigns — 77.7% of observed tool usage. The reliance on living-off-the-land binaries continues to challenge endpoint defenders.

title: APT tooling and lateral-movement usage
description: Across observed APT campaigns, command-line interpreters and built-in admin utilities dominated. Net commands appeared in 70.2% of attacks, PsExec in 66.5%, and network scanners in 54.2% — underscoring the durability of LOLBin tradecraft.

title: Industrial sector share of ransomware posts
description: The industrial sector recorded 890 victim posts — 36.57% of sector-specific ransomware activity — making it the most targeted vertical of the period. Disruption leverage from operational downtime makes industrial firms a recurring extortion target.

title: United States share of ransomware victims
description: Approximately 1,285 ransomware victims posted by attackers were located in the United States — roughly 55% of geo-identified posts. U.S. exposure continues to drive global ransomware economics.

title: Top countries by APT detections
description: Türkiye and the United States received the most APT detections during the period, with Ukraine, Israel, and Taiwan also heavily represented amid active geopolitical flashpoints. The ranking reflects relative volume from Trellix telemetry.

title: Pro-Iranian hacktivist groups mobilized
description: Following the June 2025 Israel-Iran escalation, more than 35 pro-Iranian hacktivist groups coordinated DDoS campaigns, data leaks, and disinformation operations against Israeli military, government, and critical infrastructure targets.

title: Leading ransomware groups by victim share
description: Qilin led the period with 13.45% of ransomware activity, ahead of Akira, DragonForce, Play, and a revived LockBit 5. The top 5 collectively accounted for only 39.86% of attacks, reflecting a fragmented ecosystem.

title: APT command interpreter usage: Cmd vs PowerShell
description: Across APT campaigns Cmd appeared in 48.7% and PowerShell in 47.3% of observed activity. The near-even split highlights continued attacker preference for native Windows interpreters to evade detection.

title: China-aligned APT activity around Taiwan Strait
description: Trellix observed a significant April 2025 spike in China-affiliated threat actor activity coinciding with naval exercises and ADIZ incursions. Activity declined sharply in May and leveled through August.

title: First publicly reported AI-powered infostealer
description: LameHug, disclosed in July 2025 and attributed to APT28 with moderate confidence, integrates an LLM for dynamic command generation. It was deployed operationally against Ukrainian organizations, marking a step-change in AI weaponization.

title: AI-driven threat indicators over time
description: Trellix observed a significant increase in AI-driven tools compared to earlier 2024 and 2025 quarters, including AI-generated ransomware on GitHub and AI-augmented phishing. The trend reflects the report's core 'AI inflection point' thesis.

title: Sectors hit by APT activity
description: Across the 540,974 detections and 1,221 campaigns, Trellix observed targeting across 14 sectors. The breadth confirms that no major vertical is outside the scope of state-aligned operations.

title: Monthly ransomware victim posts (Apr-Sep 2025)
description: Ransomware leak-site activity rebounded sharply after RansomHub's April collapse, with Qilin and DragonForce absorbing affiliates. August 2025 marked the peak before a modest September moderation, contributing to a total of 3,280 posts.

title: DPRK IT-worker insider threat highlighted
description: Trellix highlighted the North Korean IT worker campaign targeting American organizations. State-sponsored operatives infiltrate U.S. companies through legitimate employment, shifting from traditional malware to 'malware-less' insider operations.

title: IDC on actionable threat intelligence
description: Frank Dickson, IDC's VP for Security & Trust, frames the report's emphasis on operational threat intelligence as a strategic imperative for defenders facing converging financial and geopolitical threats.
quote: "The evolving cyber landscape demands organizations adopt actionable threat intelligence approaches."

title: Social engineering drove 36% of all incidents
description: Social engineering was the dominant intrusion method across Unit 42's incident response caseload between May 2024 and May 2025. It overtook traditional technical exploitation by targeting human workflows and trust systems.

title: Domain admin in under 40 minutes
description: One documented case saw an attacker reach domain administrator access in less than 40 minutes using only built-in tools. The intrusion relied on social engineering of help desk staff rather than malware.

title: 350 GB exfiltrated via help desk deception
description: A single help desk impersonation case enabled an attacker to obtain an MFA reset and laterally exfiltrate more than 350 GB of data without triggering EDR. The intrusion used no malware, relying entirely on legitimate administrative tools.

title: ClickFix used in 8+ confirmed IR cases
description: Between May 2024 and May 2025, ClickFix served as the initial access vector in at least eight confirmed incident response cases. The technique uses fake browser alerts, fraudulent update prompts, and drive-by downloads.

title: 700+ incident response cases analyzed
description: The report draws from more than 700 incident response engagements handled between May 2024 and May 2025. Affected clients ranged from organizations with fewer than 50 personnel to Fortune 500 and Global 2000 enterprises.

title: 90 minutes from RAT install to staged exfiltration
description: In a retail-sector ClickFix case, a fake update prompt led an employee to install a remote access Trojan. Within 90 minutes the attacker had captured order management credentials and staged outbound data transfers.

title: Why social engineering works
description: The report's closing assessment frames social engineering as a systemic, identity-centric threat rather than a sophistication problem. Defenders must move beyond traditional user awareness toward layered technical controls and zero-trust verification.
quote: "Social engineering works not because attackers are sophisticated, but because people still trust too easily, compromising organizational security."

title: 66% of social engineering targeted privileged accounts
description: Where social engineering was the initial access vector, two-thirds of attacks aimed directly at privileged accounts. Attackers concentrate on identities with the broadest blast radius.

title: 23% used callback or voice-based techniques
description: Nearly a quarter of social engineering intrusions involved callback or voice-based vectors such as vishing. This includes help desk calls and impersonation of executives by phone.

title: 60% of social engineering led to data exposure
description: Social engineering attacks resulted in data exposure in 60% of cases, 16 points higher than the overall incident rate of 44%. Exposure included direct exfiltration, credential theft, and unauthorized system access.

title: ~60% of BEC cases caused data exposure
description: Roughly half of social engineering incidents were business email compromises, and nearly 60% of all BEC cases produced data exposure. Threat actors moved quickly from access to exfiltration or credential harvesting.

title: 73% of affected orgs in North America
description: Approximately 73% of organizations in the Unit 42 IR caseload were headquartered in North America, with the remaining 27% spread across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia-Pacific. The dataset spans 49 unique countries.

title: Initial access vectors among social engineering intrusions
description: Within social engineering-driven intrusions, phishing accounted for 65% of cases. The remaining 35% used less conventional methods including SEO poisoning, malvertising, smishing, and MFA bombing.

labels: Other (SEO poisoning, malvertising, smishing, MFA bombing)

title: Social engineering tactic share by case
description: Among social engineering intrusions, 66% targeted privileged accounts, 45% used impersonation of internal personnel to build trust, and 23% involved callback or voice-based techniques. Tactics frequently overlap within the same incident.

title: Data exposure: social engineering vs all incidents
description: Social engineering intrusions produced data exposure in 60% of cases compared with 44% across all incidents — a 16 percentage point gap. The delta reflects how identity-based access accelerates the path to exfiltration.

title: Affected organizations by region
description: Unit 42 IR clients spanned 49 countries, with North America accounting for roughly 73% and the remaining 27% split across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia-Pacific. The geography reflects Unit 42's caseload, not global incident distribution.

title: Industries most impacted by social engineering
description: Manufacturing was the most impacted sector when isolating for social engineering, followed by high technology, healthcare, finance, professional services, retail, and state/federal government. The list reflects relative case concentration in Unit 42's IR engagements.

title: AI-enabled attacker tooling: three layers
description: Unit 42 categorizes attacker AI tooling into automation (rule-based intrusion acceleration), generative AI (human-like email/voice/chat content), and agentic AI (autonomous multi-step task execution). Automation is most prevalent today; agentic AI adoption remains limited but growing.

title: Six contributing factors to successful intrusions
description: Unit 42 identified six recurring patterns enabling social engineering success: missed alert escalation, failure to action alerts, insufficient EDR/endpoint logging, lack of centralized AV/EDR and tamper protection, weak or absent MFA, and excessive permissions.

title: Common ClickFix payload families
description: ClickFix campaigns favored off-the-shelf credential-harvesting malware including RedLine and Lumma infostealers, Lampion banking Trojan, and follow-on remote access Trojans. Most payloads are not novel — attackers change delivery and timing rather than tooling.

title: Attribution: financially motivated and nation-state mix
description: Unit 42 attributes most social engineering intrusions to financially motivated cybercrime groups such as Muddled Libra, alongside nation-state operations from Iran-affiliated Agent Serpens and North Korean synthetic-insider campaigns posing as remote employees.
quote: "Nearly all social engineering intrusions between May 2024 and May 2025 were financially motivated, with threat actors seeking to monetize access through data theft, extortion, ransomware, or credential resale."

title: 1 in 3 incidents used non-phishing social engineering
description: More than one third of incidents involved non-phishing techniques including SEO poisoning, fake system prompts, and help desk manipulation. The mix is broadening beyond email-based lures.

title: 49 countries represented in IR caseload
description: Affected organizations were headquartered in 49 unique countries, reflecting Unit 42's global incident response footprint. Caseload composition ranges from sub-50-person organizations to Fortune 500 and Global 2000 enterprises.

title: 12,195 confirmed breaches analyzed
description: The 2025 DBIR analyzed 22,052 real-world security incidents, of which 12,195 were confirmed data breaches, the highest number ever examined in a single edition. Victims spanned 139 countries.

title: Third-party involvement doubled to 30% of breaches
description: Third-party involvement was found in 30% of all breaches analyzed in the 2025 DBIR, roughly double the 15% reported in the 2024 report. The cover graphic for this year's report is centered on the topic, with Snowflake, Change Healthcare, CDK Global and Blue Yonder all flagged as illustrative supply-chain cases.

title: Ransomware present in 44% of breaches
description: Ransomware, with or without encryption, was a component of 44% of breaches reviewed in this year's dataset, up from 32% in the prior year, a 37% relative increase. On the incident side, Ransomware was present in 31% of cases, up from 14%.

title: Median ransom paid fell to $115K
description: The median amount paid to ransomware groups in 2024 dropped to $115,000, down from $150,000 the prior year. The drop is partially attributed to the 64% of victim organizations that did not pay the ransom, up from 50% two years ago.

title: 64% of ransomware victims refused to pay
description: According to Verizon's ransomware negotiation data contributors, 64% of victim organizations did not pay the ransom in 2024, up from 50% two years prior. Blockchain analysis from peers showed ransomware payments dropped 35% overall.

title: State-sponsored actors double-dipping for cash
description: Verizon highlights that Espionage-motivated breaches nearly tripled (a 163% increase) this year and that state-sponsored actors also pursue financially motivated activity to fund operations.
quote: "Espionage was not the only thing state-sponsored actors were interested in—approximately 28% of incidents involving those actors had a Financial motive. There has been media speculation that this may be a case of the threat actors double-dipping to pad their compensation."

title: Any device can be an edge device
description: Edge device and VPN exploitation jumped from 3% to 22% of vulnerability-based initial access vectors. The DBIR's wry framing underscores how widespread the edge attack surface has become.
quote: "All in all, those findings reinforce the old adage that 'any device can be an edge device if you are brave enough.'"

title: Vulnerability exploitation hit 20% of breaches
description: Exploitation of vulnerabilities as an initial access vector reached 20% of breaches, a 34% relative increase from the prior year. Edge devices and VPNs accounted for 22% of that vulnerability activity, up almost eight-fold from 3% last year.

title: Median 5 days to mass-exploit CISA KEV bugs
description: The median gap between CVE publication and addition to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog held at 5 days. For Verizon's edge-device subset, the median was zero days—9 of the 17 sampled CVEs hit the KEV list on or before their CVE publication date.

title: Humans still in 60% of breaches
description: Even as vulnerability exploitation rose sharply, the human element remained a 6-in-10 factor across breaches reviewed by Verizon.
quote: "We see the human involvement in breaches at 60% this year, as opposed to 61% last year, which equates to approximately the same thing within our usual 95% confidence level tolerance."

title: Initial access vectors in breaches
description: Verizon's refined initial-access analysis (Figure 5/16) shows the three dominant vectors in non-Error, non-Misuse breaches (n=9,891). Credential abuse remains on top, vulnerability exploitation has overtaken phishing, and the gap between them keeps narrowing.
comparison: Use of stolen creds down from 31%

title: Initial access vectors over time
description: Stolen credentials, vulnerability exploitation and phishing each plotted across the last four DBIR datasets. The 2025 view reflects Verizon's reclassification that removed overlap between credential abuse and exploitation, with vulnerability exploitation rising fast and phishing flat at ~15%.

title: Edge / VPN share of vulnerability exploitation
description: Edge devices and VPNs ballooned as a target of vulnerability-based access between the 2024 and 2025 datasets, almost an eight-fold jump. Verizon flags this as the defining shift behind the rise of System Intrusion and Espionage breaches.

series.name: Edge / VPN share of exploit-vuln vector

title: Remediation status of CVEs by vulnerability type
description: Verizon's vulnerability-management partners tracked remediation outcomes across edge-device CVEs, full CISA KEV entries and all scanned vulnerabilities. Edge-device bugs were patched more aggressively than other classes, but a large unremediated tail remains.

title: Ransomware share of breaches: SMB vs. large org
description: Ransomware shows up in 88% of SMB breaches compared to 39% in large organizations, hammering the long-held assumption that ransomware crews focus on large enterprises. SMBs accounted for nearly 4x more breach victims than large orgs in the dataset.

title: Espionage-motivated breaches by industry
description: Espionage motivation surged across industries in the 2025 dataset. Manufacturing went from 3% to 20%, Healthcare from 1% to 16%, Retail from 1% to 9%, and Financial from 5% to 12%, reflecting both new contributor visibility and real geopolitical pressure.

title: State-sponsored actor motives in incidents
description: Across 1,892 incidents tied to state-sponsored actors, Espionage dominates but financial motivation is also surprisingly common. Verizon notes this overlap supports the 'double-dipping' theory of state-backed crews monetising their access.

title: 46% of compromised corporate logins on non-managed devices
description: Verizon's infostealer analysis found that 46% of compromised systems with corporate logins were non-managed devices hosting both personal and business credentials. The DBIR ties this directly to BYOD risk and lack of enforced device policies.

title: 54% of ransomware victims pre-exposed in infostealer logs
description: Correlating ransomware leak-site disclosures with infostealer logs and marketplace postings, Verizon found 54% of ransomware victim domains appeared in credential dumps, and 40% of those entries included corporate email addresses, suggesting access-broker tradecraft.

title: AI-written malicious emails doubled to ~10%
description: An email-security partner's research, reproduced by the DBIR, shows the share of malicious emails that appear synthetically generated has roughly doubled over the past two years—from ~5% to ~10%—coinciding with the popularization of LLM chat tools.

title: Employees accessing GenAI outside corporate policy
description: Browser-monitoring data shows 15% of employees routinely access GenAI tools on corporate devices. Of those, 72% use non-corporate emails and 17% use a corporate email without integrated SSO, leaving only ~11% on properly sanctioned accounts.

title: $6.3B transferred via BEC in 2024
description: Per FBI IC3 figures cited by Verizon, more than $6.3 billion was transferred as part of Business Email Compromise scams in 2024 across ~19,000 complaints. The median amount extracted from victims has stabilized around $50,000, with 88% of proceeds moved via wire transfer.

title: Phishing reporting rate: trained vs. untrained
description: Across ~7,000 organizations running phishing simulations, employees who had recent (within 30 days) security awareness training reported phishing emails at 21%, vs. a 5% base rate without recent training—a 4x relative lift, even as click rates barely moved.

title: Microsoft 365 MFA bypass by attack type
description: Analysis of Microsoft 365 logs from a managed-security data contributor shows token theft is the most common MFA-bypass technique observed in attacks, followed by MFA-interrupt and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing.

title: Median dwell time fell to 24 days
description: For breaches not disclosed by the threat actor themselves, the median dwell time improved to 24 days in the 2025 dataset, down from roughly 30 days reported in the 2023 DBIR. Verizon notes the change is statistically modest but operationally meaningful.

title: Confirmed breaches by region
description: Breach counts by world region in the 2025 DBIR. EMEA topped the list with 5,321 confirmed breaches, followed by Northern America (2,867), APAC (1,374) and LATAM/Caribbean (413).

title: APAC: System Intrusion overwhelms breaches
description: APAC's threat landscape became dramatically dominated by System Intrusion in the 2025 DBIR, jumping from 39% to 83% of breaches. Social Engineering and Basic Web Application Attacks declined as a proportion of the whole.

title: Basic Web App Attack motives flipped to Espionage
description: For the first time, Espionage became the top motive in Basic Web Application Attacks at 62%, displacing Financial motivation. State actors are increasingly leaning on credential abuse to walk in through the front door.

title: Ransomware in 30% of Public Sector breaches
description: Ransomware was present in 30% of Public Sector breaches, with about 43% of those victims being U.S. local governments. The pattern impacts federal, state and council-level government bodies across regions.

title: DDoS bandwidth up ~1,000% since 2018
description: Verizon's DDoS contributors show a 200%+ growth in median attack size since 2018 and roughly a 1,000% increase in the upper bound of bits-per-second. Finance, Manufacturing and Professional Services together account for more than 75% of DoS cases.

title: AI named top driver of cybersecurity change
description: AI is anticipated to be the most significant driver of change in cybersecurity in the year ahead, according to 94% of survey respondents. The Forum frames AI as both a force multiplier for defenders and a catalyst for attackers in 2026.

title: AI vulnerabilities are the fastest-growing cyber risk
description: 87% of respondents identified AI-related vulnerabilities as the fastest-growing cyber risk over the course of 2025, ranking the category ahead of cyber-enabled fraud, supply chain disruption and ransomware.

title: Share of organizations assessing AI tool security nearly doubled
description: Organizations with a process to assess AI tool security before deployment rose from 37% in 2025 to 64% in 2026, indicating rapid maturation of AI governance practices year over year.

title: Perceived increase in cyber risks over the past year
description: Survey respondents rated which cyber risks increased in 2025. AI vulnerabilities (87%) and cyber-enabled fraud and phishing (77%) lead a broad-based perception of escalating threats.

title: Geopolitical attacks lead cyber risk mitigation strategies
description: 64% of organizations are accounting for geopolitically motivated cyberattacks - such as disruption of critical infrastructure or espionage - making geopolitics the top factor influencing risk mitigation in 2026.

title: Year-over-year strategy shifts due to geopolitical volatility
description: The share of organizations changing their cybersecurity strategy because of geopolitical volatility declined from 93% in 2023 to 66% in 2026, suggesting the initial adaptation wave has passed even as geopolitics remains the top risk factor.

title: Largest organizations have re-tooled cyber strategy for geopolitics
description: 91% of the largest organizations (>100,000 employees) have changed their cybersecurity strategies due to geopolitical volatility, compared to 59% of those with under 1,000 employees - showing scale-driven divergence in resilience investment.

title: Low confidence in national cyber preparedness rising
description: 31% of survey participants express lack of confidence in their nation's ability to respond effectively to major cyber incidents, up from 26% last year, signaling growing uncertainty around critical infrastructure protection.

title: Regional confidence in national response to critical infrastructure attacks
description: Confidence varies sharply across regions. MENA respondents express the highest confidence in their country's ability to protect critical infrastructure (84%), while Latin America and the Caribbean trail at just 13%.

title: Cyber-enabled fraud is reaching households
description: 73% of respondents reported that they or someone in their network had been personally affected by cyber-enabled fraud in the past 12 months, with phishing/vishing/smishing the most common attack type (62%).

title: Most common cyber-enabled fraud types reported by respondents
description: Phishing/vishing/smishing (62%), invoice or payment fraud (37%) and identity theft (32%) lead the categories of cyber-enabled fraud experienced personally or in respondents' networks.

title: Regional prevalence of cyber-enabled fraud exposure
description: Sub-Saharan Africa leads exposure with 82% of respondents reporting they or their network were affected, followed by North America at 79%. East Asia & Pacific trails at 59%, reflecting differing fraud ecosystems.

title: CEOs' top genAI security concerns
description: CEOs identify data leaks (30%) and the advancement of adversarial capabilities (28%) as the most significant security concerns related to generative AI - the two risks stand clearly above technical security (15%) and governance complexity (13%).

title: Reversal in top genAI concern: data leaks now lead
description: In 2026, data leaks via genAI rose to 34% (from 22% in 2025) while advancement of adversarial capabilities fell to 29% (from 47% in 2025) - a striking reversal in the top genAI cybersecurity concern.

title: AI is now standard in defensive operations
description: 77% of organizations have adopted AI for cybersecurity, primarily for phishing detection (52%), intrusion and anomaly response (46%), and user-behaviour analytics (40%).

title: Top AI-for-cybersecurity use cases
description: Among the 77% of organizations using AI for cybersecurity, phishing detection (52%) and intrusion/anomaly response (46%) lead use cases, followed by automated security operations (43%) and user-behaviour analytics (40%).

title: Cyber resilience self-assessment 2024-2026
description: Organizations reporting resilience that exceeds requirements doubled from 9% in 2025 to 19% in 2026, while those reporting insufficient resilience held steady, indicating concentrated improvement at the top end.

title: Greatest challenges to organizational cyber resilience
description: The rapidly evolving threat landscape (61%), third-party and supply chain vulnerabilities (46%), and the cybersecurity skills shortage (45%) are the top three barriers to building resilience in 2026.

title: Technologies with the greatest cybersecurity impact in next 12 months
description: AI/ML tops the list at 94%, far ahead of cloud (61%), quantum (37%), autonomous systems (26%), decentralized tech (20%), and space technologies (9%) - confirming AI and cloud as the dominant focus areas.

title: OT security barely reaches the board
description: Only 16% of organizations with industrial environments report OT security issues to their boards, and just 20% maintain a dedicated OT security team - underscoring persistent governance gaps in cyber-physical security.

title: Most security leaders see regulations as effective
description: 74% of respondents hold a positive view of the effectiveness of cyber-related regulations - citing board awareness (58%) and posture improvement (55%) as top benefits, even as multinationals struggle with consistency.

title: Supply chain risk now top barrier for large companies
description: 65% of large companies by revenue cite third-party and supply chain vulnerabilities as their greatest challenge to cyber resilience, up from 54% in 2025 - reflecting heightened sensitivity after major 2025 incidents.

title: Jaguar Land Rover cyberattack triggered $2.5B UK economic loss
description: The August 2025 cyberattack on Jaguar Land Rover halted production for five weeks, affected 5,000+ suppliers, drove a ~25% revenue drop and an estimated GBP 1.9 billion ($2.5B) in wider UK economic losses. Direct cyber-related costs reached GBP 196M ($260M).

title: Average significant UK cyberattack costs ~$250K
description: Per UK government research cited by WEF, the average significant cyberattack costs businesses nearly GBP 195,000 ($250,000), which scales to an estimated GBP 14.7B ($19.4B) in annual economic losses nationally.

title: How organizations address supply chain cyber risk
description: While 66% of organizations assess supplier security maturity and 65% involve security in procurement, only 27% simulate cyber incidents with partners and 33% comprehensively map their ecosystem - showing checkbox compliance over dynamic management.

title: Public sector lags private on cyber resilience
description: 23% of public-sector organizations report having insufficient cyber-resilience capabilities, compared to just 11% in the private sector - a structural inequity highlighted by recent infrastructure incidents.

title: AI-enabled cybersecurity tool adoption by company size and sector
description: AI for cybersecurity is dominated by large enterprises (93% adoption, >$5.5B revenue) and medium firms (83%), while small companies (78%), the public sector (45%) and NGOs (70%) lag - deepening cyber inequity.

title: Regional cyber skills gap: LATAM and Sub-Saharan Africa hit hardest
description: 65% of organizations in Latin America and the Caribbean and 63% in Sub-Saharan Africa report missing critical people and skills for cybersecurity objectives, compared to 35% in South Asia and 37% in Europe & Central Asia.

title: State-linked crypto-exchange breach: $1.5B in losses
description: In 2025, a major crypto-exchange breach attributed to a state-linked threat group resulted in losses exceeding $1.5 billion, with nearly a fifth of stolen funds rapidly converted into unrecoverable assets.

title: 99% of international data traffic flows through undersea cables
description: Per ITU Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin, 99% of international data traffic flows through undersea cables, yet only 18% of organizations account for undersea cables in cyber risk mitigation.

title: Cybersecurity is a frontier of collaboration
description: From the Executive Summary, the WEF frames cybersecurity as inherently collaborative even in a fragmented world - a recurring theme across the 2026 outlook.
quote: "Cybersecurity is a frontier where collaboration remains not only possible, but powerful - a reminder that, even amid fragmentation, economic strain and uncertainty, collective action can drive progress for all."

title: IBM CEO on agentic AI for defenders
description: Arvind Krishna, CEO of IBM, on the necessity of using every available tool - including agentic AI - to defend against criminal abuse of cyber infrastructure.
quote: "Criminals are always willing to use all possible ways to get access to value, much of which is contained in the cyber infrastructure. Consequently, to stay ahead, those of us who defend must use every tool at our disposal - which now includes agentic AI."

title: Operation Serengeti 2.0: $97.4M recovered, 1,209 arrests
description: INTERPOL's Operation Serengeti 2.0 - coordinated with 18 African countries and the UK to tackle ransomware, online scams and BEC - led to 1,209 arrests and the recovery of $97.4 million in 2025.

title: Lumma Infostealer disruption: 394,000 infected machines
description: Europol and Microsoft jointly disrupted the Lumma infostealer ecosystem, affecting 394,000 infected machines and seizing 1,300+ malicious domains - one of the largest 2025 infostealer takedowns.

title: Norwegian hydropower dam hack released 500 L/s for 4 hours
description: In April 2025, a Norwegian hydropower dam was hacked, opening a floodgate and releasing 500 litres of water per second for four hours - described by officials as a deliberate act of sabotage on critical infrastructure.

title: Phishing is down but more targeted
description: ThreatLabz frames 2024 as the year phishing volume retreated while quality, precision, and psychological manipulation reached new heights. Attackers abandoned spray-and-pray volumes for hyper-personalized, AI-enabled campaigns against high-value targets.
quote: "While global phishing volume declined, the quality, precision, and psychological manipulation behind attacks reached new heights."

title: Blocked phishing transactions analyzed
description: ThreatLabz analyzed over 2 billion blocked phishing transactions observed across the Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange between January and December 2024. The dataset underpins all geographic, industry, and brand-imitation rankings in the report.

title: Global phishing volume drop
description: Global phishing transactions fell 20% year-over-year in 2024, driven largely by stronger email authentication (DMARC, SPF, DKIM) and sender verification by major mailbox providers. The decline masks a sharper pivot to targeted, multi-channel social engineering.

title: US phishing decline (still #1 target)
description: Phishing volumes targeting the United States dropped 31.8% in 2024, yet the US remained the world's most-targeted country. The decline is attributed to widespread DMARC enforcement and Google's sender verification program.

title: Unauthenticated emails blocked by Google
description: Google's sender verification program blocked 265 billion unauthenticated emails over the year, a key driver behind the global volume decline and the steep US drop. ThreatLabz cites it as evidence that ecosystem-wide email authentication is finally moving the needle.

title: Education sector phishing surge
